title: Central limit theorem
summary: For i.i.d. observations with finite variance, the standardized sample mean converges in distribution to N(0, 1). A large sample size is a rule of thumb for using the approximation, not a hypothesis of the theorem. Finite variance is required.
intuition:
The central limit theorem is a statement about the sample mean, not about one observation. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2>0$. The sample mean $\bar X$ has exact mean $\mu$ and exact variance $\sigma^2/n$. Those two moments do not need a limit. What needs a limit is the shape. The standardized mean

$$
\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar X-\mu)}{\sigma}
$$

converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$ as $n\to\infty$. Equivalently, $\bar X$ is approximately $N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$ when $n$ is large. The denominator of the standardized mean is $\sigma$, and the standard deviation of $\bar X$ itself is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.

Finite variance is part of the hypothesis. If the variance is infinite, this normal limit need not hold. The phrase 'n at least 30' is a classroom rule of thumb for when the approximation is often usable. It is not a line in the theorem, and it is not a switch that makes $\bar X$ exactly normal. If the observations are themselves normal, the sample mean is exactly normal for every $n$, and the theorem is not needed.

A continuity correction is a small shift, often by half a unit, used when a normal curve approximates a lattice distribution such as a binomial count. It can improve a numerical approximation. It is not the content of the central limit theorem, and this lesson does not turn on it.

definitions.body: If $X_i$ are i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and finite positive variance $\sigma^2$, then $\sqrt{n}(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$.
The exact standard deviation of $\bar X$ is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. It is the scale used in the normal approximation, not $\sigma$ and not $\sigma/n$.
Advice such as '$n$ at least 30' is a rough guide to the approximation. It is not a hypothesis and not a conclusion of the theorem.
An optional half-unit shift when a normal approximation is applied to a count. Mention it as a refinement. It is not a substitute for the limit statement.

formulas.name: Limit
formulas.note: i.i.d. observations with finite variance $\sigma^2$. The limit is standard normal.

formulas.name: Approximate sampling law
formulas.note: The variance $\sigma^2/n$ is exact for i.i.d. data. The normal shape is the approximation, unless the data are already normal.

properties: The theorem assumes i.i.d. observations with finite variance. Without a finite variance, the same normal limit is not guaranteed.
The standardized sample mean $\sqrt{n}(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma$ is the object that converges to $N(0,1)$. The sample mean itself converges to a point mass at $\mu$ by the law of large numbers.
For any n, i.i.d. data with finite variance satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\bar X]=\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$ exactly. The CLT adds the approximate shape.
A threshold such as $n\ge 30$ is a rule of thumb, not a theorem. Normal data have an exactly normal sample mean at every sample size.
A continuity correction may be used when approximating a discrete count by a normal curve. It is an optional refinement of the approximation, not the statement of the CLT.

examples.title: Mean 50, variance 16, sample of 64
examples.prompt: Observations are i.i.d. with mean 50 and variance 16. The sample size is $n=64$. Find the mean and standard deviation of $\bar X$, and the CLT z-score of the value 51.
steps: The variance is finite, so the theorem applies. The sample mean has exact mean 50 and exact variance $16/64=1/4$, hence standard deviation $1/2$.
The standardized value at 51 is $(51-50)/(1/2)=2$. Under the CLT, $P(\bar X>51)$ is approximately $1-\Phi(2)$.
The number 64 is large enough that the rule of thumb is comfortable, but '64 is at least 30' is not what makes the variance equal to $1/4$. That equality is exact.
examples.answer: The sample mean has mean 50 and standard deviation $1/2$. The z-score of 51 is 2.

examples.title: A fair-coin proportion
examples.prompt: Let $\bar X$ be the proportion of heads in 100 independent fair coin tosses. Approximate the z-score of the event $\bar X>0.6$.
steps: Each toss is Bernoulli($1/2$), with mean $1/2$ and finite variance $1/4$. The sample size is 100.
The standard deviation of $\bar X$ is $\sqrt{(1/4)/100}=1/20=0.05$. This is exact.

The z-score of 0.6 is $(0.6-0.5)/0.05=2$. The CLT says $P(\bar X>0.6)\approx 1-\Phi(2)$. A continuity correction would shift a count by half a toss before standardizing. It is available and it is not required to see that the standardized distance is about 2.
examples.answer: The z-score is 2. The normal approximation uses mean $0.5$ and standard deviation $0.05$.

traps: Dropping the finite-variance hypothesis. The classical normal limit is for i.i.d. data with finite $\sigma^2$. Infinite variance can produce a different limit.
Treating '$n\ge 30$' as a theorem. It is a rule of thumb. It does not make a non-normal sample mean exactly normal, and normal data do not need it.
Using $\sigma/n$ as the standard deviation of the sample mean. The exact standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. For $\sigma=8$ and $n=100$ that is $0.8$, not $0.08$.
Making a continuity correction the whole method. It is an optional half-unit adjustment for lattice distributions. The theorem is the normal limit for the standardized sample mean.
python:
from fractions import Fraction
assert Fraction(16, 64) == Fraction(1, 4)
assert (51 - 50) / Fraction(1, 2) == 2
assert (Fraction(3, 5) - Fraction(1, 2)) / Fraction(1, 20) == 2
assert Fraction(8, 10) == Fraction(4, 5)
assert (Fraction(11, 2) - 4) / Fraction(1, 2) == 3
assert (Fraction(10, 2)) ** 2 == 25
print(2, float(Fraction(4, 5)), 25)

questions.stem: Observations are i.i.d. with standard deviation $\sigma=8$. For a sample of size $n=100$, the standard deviation of the sample mean is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $0.8$.

The standard deviation of $\bar X$ is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=8/\sqrt{100}=8/10=0.8$. This identity is exact when the variance is finite. It is not an output of the large-sample limit. Option C divides by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$. Option B forgets to scale. Option D multiplies.

questions.stem: Observations are i.i.d. with mean 4 and variance 25. The sample size is $n=100$. The CLT z-score of $\bar X=5.5$ is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $3$.

The standard deviation of the sample mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=5/10=0.5$. The z-score is $(5.5-4)/0.5=3$. Finite variance 25 is what lets the classical theorem apply. Option B is the raw difference $1.5$. Option C divides $1.5$ by $\sigma=5$ instead of by the standard error. Option D multiplies the difference by $\sqrt{n}$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of the classical central limit theorem for a sample mean?
options: It assumes i.i.d. observations with finite variance.
A cutoff such as $n\ge 30$ is a rule of thumb, not part of the theorem.
The same $N(0,1)$ limit holds for every i.i.d. sequence, including sequences with infinite variance.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The classical statement needs a finite variance, and the standardized sample mean is what converges to standard normal. Sample-size cutoffs are rules of thumb. Option D is false: infinite variance is outside the hypothesis, and the normal limit can fail.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: For i.i.d. data with finite variance, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$ holds exactly, not only in the limit.
A continuity correction is an optional refinement when a normal curve approximates a count.
The sample mean of i.i.d. normal observations is exactly normal for every sample size.
The central limit theorem says that a single observation is approximately normal whenever the population is not.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The variance formula for the sample mean is exact under independence and finite variance. A continuity correction is optional and is not the theorem. Normal observations have a normal sample mean at every $n$, with variance $\sigma^2/n$. Option D reverses the theorem: the CLT is about averages, and it does not make one draw from a non-normal population normal.

questions.stem: Observations are i.i.d. with standard deviation $\sigma=10$. The standard deviation of the sample mean equals 2. Enter the sample size $n$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **25**.

Solve $10/\sqrt{n}=2$. Then $\sqrt{n}=5$ and $n=25$. The variance of the sample mean is $\sigma^2/n=100/25=4$, whose square root is 2. This uses the exact standard-error formula. It does not use a normal table.
